# Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization

Sirui Chen Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Email: [sirui6@illinois.edu](mailto:)    Zhining Liu
Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Chao Zhang
Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology    Jingrui He
Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Zheng Li
Affiliation: Amazon

###### Abstract

LLM agents can evolve by learning from accumulated experience. Existing
approaches extract reusable external knowledge, such as skills and
memories, from experience to guide subsequent task solving, with some
further internalizing this knowledge through model training. However,
different ways of analyzing and transforming the same experience can
yield knowledge with substantially different utility, even when the
resulting guidance appears reasonable. Inspired by consistency
regularization, we identify consistent utility gains across different
ways of analyzing the same experience, rather than relying on any single
way of analyzing it. We introduce SPLICE, a framework for
consistency-regularized knowledge-model co-evolution. It constructs
evolution views by perturbing how the same experience is analyzed,
producing different knowledge candidates. Knowledge updates are then
guided by common gain, which accounts for utility gains and their
consistency across views. During model evolution, self-distillation
internalizes the evolved knowledge alongside reinforcement learning,
using knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation as a
contrastive reference. The two processes interleave, with model updates
driving further knowledge evolution. Experiments across diverse domains
show that SPLICE outperforms knowledge evolution and model training
baselines by up to 7.1 and 4.6 points in average accuracy, while its
evolved knowledge reduces output tokens per correct solution by up to
44% and transfers across model sizes and families.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Model (LLM) agents accumulate experience whenever they
reason, use tools, and interact with the environment. For this
experience to support continual improvement, an agent must identify
useful guidance and reuse it in future tasks. This motivates knowledge
evolution, through which agents extract and revise external knowledge,
such as skills and memories, from their experience ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8); [Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)). Such knowledge can
also be internalized into model parameters through policy training ([Lu
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Lu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10); [He et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib13)). The updated model then generates new experience for
further knowledge evolution, allowing knowledge and the model to
co-evolve ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [He et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib12)). External knowledge thus serves as a _medium for
agent evolution_, connecting accumulated experience with subsequent task
solving and model learning.

However, knowledge derived from the same experience can differ
substantially depending on which evidence is selected and how it is
interpreted. For example, analyzing a purchase of the wrong size can
yield guidance to include size requirements in queries or verify the
selected size before purchase. On a product page that lists the
requested size but defaults to another option, the first rule leaves the
incorrect selection unchanged, while the second corrects it.
Consequently, different ways of analyzing and transforming the same
experience can yield knowledge with substantially different utility.
Recent studies similarly find that even seemingly reasonable criteria
for analyzing and transforming experience can yield less useful
knowledge ([Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)), and that plausible
knowledge can even underperform using no knowledge at all ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib14); [Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)). This raises a
central question: _how can experience be effectively transformed into
generalizable knowledge to support agentic evolution?_

To tackle this problem, we draw inspiration from consistency
regularization
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")).
This approach encourages consistent predictions for the same input under
random parameter perturbations ([Ni et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Wu et
al., 2021](#bib.bib17)). This reduces prediction sensitivity to such
perturbations and can improve generalization. Similarly, we view the
transformation of experience into knowledge as a function parameterized
by textual instructions, whose perturbations define different evolution
views. Here, consistency concerns utility: when different views produce
distinct knowledge yet yield consistent positive gains on the same
tasks, this suggests that the benefits are not specific to a single
evolution view. Rather than relying on any single analysis, we therefore
use utility consistency across evolution views to guide knowledge
evolution toward more generalizable knowledge.

We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized
knowledge-model co-evolution. During knowledge evolution, it perturbs
how the same experience is analyzed and transformed, creating _evolution
views_ that each produce a knowledge candidate. Each candidate is
evaluated through task replay, and a _common gain_ is calculated by
combining utility gain with cross-view consistency. A knowledge
optimizer then updates the current knowledge using the candidates and
replay trajectories from tasks with the highest common gains. During
model evolution, SPLICE combines GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib18))
with self-distillation to internalize the evolved knowledge. The same
replay also reveals guidance associated with consistent utility
degradation, from which we construct noisy knowledge as a contrastive
reference to highlight useful guidance in the evolved knowledge. A
token-level gate controls its contribution to retain shared useful
guidance. The two processes are interleaved, with the updated model
generating new experience for further co-evolution. We evaluate SPLICE
on four benchmarks covering math, coding, office work, and web shopping
at two model scales. Across these tasks, SPLICE consistently outperforms
knowledge evolution and model training baselines, improving average
accuracy over the strongest baseline by 3.0 points for Qwen3.5-4B and
4.6 points for Qwen3.5-9B. Notably, its evolved knowledge makes task
solving more efficient, requiring up to 44% fewer output tokens per
correct solution than the strongest baseline, and delivers larger gains
when transferred to other model sizes and families.

## 2 Preliminaries

#### Knowledge-model co-evolution.

We consider an LLM agent parameterized by $`\theta`$ and equipped with
external knowledge $`K`$, including reusable skills, tools, memories, or
environment information. Given a task $`x\sim\mathcal{D}`$, the agent
generates a trajectory $`\tau`$ using
$`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tau_{<t},K)`$, where $`\tau_{<t}`$ contains
preceding model outputs and environment feedback. The task, trajectory,
and feedback, including the reward $`R(x,\tau)`$, form the experience
$`\mathcal{E}`$. Knowledge evolution updates $`K`$ from experience
$`\mathcal{E}`$, yielding
$`\widetilde{K}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E},K;p)`$, where $`\mathcal{G}`$ is
a knowledge optimizer parameterized by textual instructions $`p`$. This
transformation typically involves analyzing trajectories and feedback,
proposing reusable guidance, and organizing and reviewing knowledge
updates. The instructions $`p`$ specify which aspects of the experience
are examined and how the resulting guidance is incorporated into $`K`$.

Model evolution then internalizes knowledge-guided behaviors into
$`\theta`$ through training. The updated model generates new experience
and can change the utility of $`K`$, measured by the model’s expected
task reward with that knowledge, informing subsequent knowledge
evolution. Co-evolution interleaves these two processes to maximize the
expected return of the final policy under the evolved knowledge,
$`J_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,K)}[R(x,\tau)]`$.

#### Group Relative Policy Optimization.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)) optimizes the policy using group-relative advantages.
For each task $`x`$, it samples $`G`$ trajectories
$`\{\tau_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G}`$ from the behavior policy
$`\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot\mid x)`$ and minimizes

|     |                                                         |                                                                     |           |                |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- | -------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum\_{g=1}^{G}\frac{1}{ | \tau\_{g} | }\sum\_{t=1}^{ | \tau\_{g} | }\min\left(\rho*{g,t}A*{g},\,\operatorname{clip}(\rho*{g,t},1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A*{g}\right)\right]+\beta\mathcal{D}\_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta),`$ |     | (1) |

where the expectation is over tasks and sampled trajectory groups. Here,
$`\rho_{g,t}`$ is the token probability ratio between $`\pi_{\theta}`$
and $`\pi_{\text{old}}`$, $`A_{g}`$ is the group-normalized advantage of
trajectory $`\tau_{g}`$, $`\varepsilon`$ is the clipping threshold, and
$`\beta`$ weights the KL penalty toward a frozen reference policy.

## 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution

We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized
knowledge-model co-evolution, illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
Knowledge evolution
(§ [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"))
uses utility consistency across evolution views to guide updates to
external knowledge. Model evolution
(§ [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"))
internalizes the evolved knowledge through GRPO and gated contrastive
self-distillation. The two processes are interleaved, with the updated
model generating new experience for further knowledge evolution.

![Refer to caption](2610.30790v1/Main_Fig.png)

Figure 2: Overview of SPLICE. Left: Knowledge evolution perturbs how the
same experience is analyzed and transformed, using common gain across
evolution views to select task experience for knowledge updates. Right:
Model evolution combines GRPO with gated contrastive self-distillation
to internalize the evolved knowledge, using noisy knowledge as a
contrastive reference.

### 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution

#### Knowledge consistency evaluation.

At each round, the LLM agent $`\pi_{\theta}`$ solves a batch of tasks
$`\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{B}`$ with the current knowledge $`K`$ to collect
experience $`\mathcal{E}`$. We then ask the knowledge optimizer
$`\mathcal{G}`$ to generate $`N`$ textual revisions of $`p`$. These
revisions can emphasize different aspects of a failure, such as planning
errors, ineffective tool use, or missed task requirements. Each revision
defines a distinct _evolution view_, which is applied to the same
$`\mathcal{E}`$ and $`K`$ to produce a knowledge candidate:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
K^{(j)}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{E},K;p\oplus\delta_{j}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`\delta_{j}`$ denotes a textual revision, and $`\oplus`$
incorporates it into $`p`$. To assess the utility of each knowledge
candidate $`K^{(j)}`$, we replay the tasks used to collect
$`\mathcal{E}`$ with that candidate, enabling direct utility comparisons
against the current knowledge $`K`$. For task $`x_{i}`$, we define
$`\Delta_{ij}`$ as the mean reward gain under $`K^{(j)}`$ relative to
the current knowledge $`K`$ across replay runs. A high observed gain
from a single candidate can reflect useful knowledge or a particularly
successful execution. We therefore select task experience supported by
consistent utility gains across evolution views, rather than choosing a
candidate solely by its average gain across tasks. For each task
$`x_{i}`$, we compute the *common gain*, which combines the mean utility
gain with an inconsistency penalty:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{C}_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Delta_{ij}}_{\text{mean gain}}-\underbrace{\frac{1}{2\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{j<\ell}|\Delta_{ij}-\Delta_{i\ell}|}_{\text{inconsistency penalty}}=\frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{j<\ell}\min(\Delta_{ij},\Delta_{i\ell}).`$ |  | (3) |

The pairwise-minimum form measures the gain shared by two evolution
views. Averaging over pairs favors tasks with gains consistently
supported across views, while discounting isolated high gains that can
reflect an occasional success or guidance specific to a particular view.
We select up to $`n`$ tasks with the highest positive common gains
($`\widehat{C}_{i}>0`$). Their trajectories provide evidence of
improvements supported across evolution views, forming the basis for the
subsequent knowledge update. The following proposition further connects
population common gain to the probability of obtaining positive utility
gains under a new evolution view.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The proof is deferred to
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Proof of Proposition ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
The bound depends on two quantities: the mean utility gain $`\mu`$ and
the utility inconsistency
$`\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|`$. The mean gain
measures the average benefit of the generated knowledge, while
inconsistency measures how much this benefit changes across evolution
views. At the same positive mean gain, lower inconsistency gives a
stronger lower bound on the probability of improvement under a new view.
We further discuss the properties of common-gain selection in detail in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

#### Knowledge evolution from common gain.

Let $`\mathcal{S}`$ denote the selected tasks,
$`\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\mathcal{E}`$ their original
experience under $`K`$, and $`\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(j)}`$ their
replay experience under $`K^{(j)}`$. The knowledge optimizer
$`\mathcal{G}`$ compares these trajectories to relate changes in
knowledge to changes in task behavior, and identifies updates supported
by consistent utility gains across evolution views, rather than simply
extracting content shared by the candidates. It consolidates these
updates into $`K`$ to produce

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{K}=\mathcal{G}\big(\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}},\{K^{(j)},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{S}}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{N},K;p^{\prime}\big),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`p^{\prime}`$ denotes the instructions for knowledge update. We
evaluate $`\widetilde{K}`$ against $`K`$ on a held-out validation set
and accept it only if validation performance improves; otherwise, $`K`$
remains unchanged. Subsequent rounds repeat this process with new
experience under the current model and knowledge.

### 3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution

A natural way to internalize the evolved knowledge $`K`$ is
self-distillation ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)), using the model
conditioned on $`K`$ as a teacher. Our knowledge evolution process can
also reveal patterns associated with consistent utility degradation.
Prior work shows that learning from negative samples can provide useful
supervision by discouraging incorrect responses ([Zhu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib21)). Motivated by these findings, we construct noisy
knowledge from these degradation patterns and use it as a contrastive
reference to complement the guidance from $`K`$ during
self-distillation.

#### Contrastive knowledge guidance.

To construct this reference, we follow the task-selection procedure in
§ [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
replacing $`\Delta_{ij}`$ with $`-\Delta_{ij}`$ when computing common
gain. This selects tasks with utility degradation consistently supported
across evolution views. For the selected tasks, the knowledge optimizer
$`\mathcal{G}`$ similarly extracts and consolidates guidance associated
with utility degradation into noisy knowledge $`K^{-}`$ for contrastive
self-distillation. We construct $`K^{-}`$ anew whenever model evolution
starts training with $`K`$, rather than evolving $`K^{-}`$ across
knowledge evolution rounds.

#### Gated knowledge internalization.

Knowledge that improves overall task performance can fail to benefit
some tasks, while knowledge associated with degradation can still
contain useful guidance. We therefore weight self-distillation by the
observed task-level benefit of $`K`$ and gate the contribution of
$`K^{-}`$ at the token level. At the start of each training batch, we
collect trajectories with and without $`K`$ for each task $`x_{i}`$
using the current policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$. Let $`\overline{R}_{i}^{K}`$
and $`\overline{R}_{i}^{\varnothing}`$ denote the mean rewards of the
two rollout groups. We define the task-level weight
$`w_{i}=\max(\overline{R}_{i}^{K}-\overline{R}_{i}^{\varnothing},0)`$,
so only tasks with positive observed gains contribute to contrastive
self-distillation, with larger gains receiving greater weight. At the
token level, we gate the contribution of $`K^{-}`$ to preserve useful
guidance shared with $`K`$. For each token $`y_{t}`$ in a trajectory
sampled without knowledge, we compare the model’s predictions under
$`K`$, $`K^{-}`$ and no knowledge on the same history. Let
$`\ell_{t}(K^{\prime})=\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x_{i},\tau_{<t},K^{\prime})`$
and $`\ell_{t}=\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x_{i},\tau_{<t})`$ denote its
log-probabilities with and without knowledge. We define the token-level
gate $`\gamma_{t}`$ and training signal $`a_{t}`$ as

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\gamma_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(-[\ell_{t}(K)-\ell_{t}][\ell_{t}(K^{-})-\ell_{t}],0,1\right),`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle a_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\sigma\!\left(\ell_{t}(K)-\ell_{t}-\gamma_{t}[\ell_{t}(K^{-})-\ell_{t}]\right)\right],`$ |  |  |

where $`\sigma`$ is a bounded, sign-preserving activation (e.g.,
$`\tanh`$), and $`\operatorname{sg}`$ stops gradients. When $`K`$ and
$`K^{-}`$ change the token probability in the same direction,
$`\gamma_{t}=0`$ and supervision comes from $`K`$ alone. When their
effects oppose each other, $`\gamma_{t}`$ controls how strongly
$`K^{-}`$ reinforces the signal from $`K`$. The activation $`\sigma`$
limits the magnitude of this signal while preserving its sign. Combining
the task-level weight with the token-level signal gives

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CSD}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}\!\left[w_{i}a_{t}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x_{i},\tau_{<t})\right],`$ |  | (7) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPLICE}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CSD}}.`$ |  |  |

Here, $`\lambda`$ balances the two losses:
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$ optimizes task reward on rollouts with
and without $`K`$, and $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CSD}}`$ internalizes $`K`$
weighted by its observed benefit.

#### Knowledge-model co-evolution in SPLICE.

Co-evolution jointly updates the agent’s external knowledge $`K`$ and
model parameters $`\theta`$. Knowledge evolution proposes updates to
$`K`$ through
Eq. [5](#S3.E5 "In Knowledge evolution from common gain. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
and model evolution uses the adopted knowledge to update $`\theta`$
through
Eq. [7](#S3.E7 "In Gated knowledge internalization. ‣ 3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
The updated model generates new trajectories and feedback that provide
experience for subsequent knowledge evolution. Since knowledge utility
depends on the task model, proposed knowledge is evaluated with respect
to the current model as training proceeds. We detail the co-evolution
procedures in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Benchmarks and baselines.

We evaluate SPLICE on four benchmarks from diverse domains:
LiveMathBench (LiveMath) ([He et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22)) for
mathematical reasoning, LiveCodeBench (LiveCode) ([Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23)) for code generation, SpreadsheetBench
(SpreadSheet) ([Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) for spreadsheet
manipulation, and WebShop ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)) for
interactive web shopping, and report accuracy (Acc.) on the test splits.
We compare SPLICE with two groups of baselines. Training-free knowledge
evolution methods, including ReasoningBank ([Ouyang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib4)), ACE ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)),
EvoSkill ([Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), and SkillOpt ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)), evolve external knowledge with the task model fixed.
Training-based methods include GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)),
which optimizes the policy with reinforcement learning, and
SkillRL ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)) and ReSkill ([He et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib12)), which co-evolve skills with the policy. We also
report the base model without knowledge. Details of the benchmarks and
baselines are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

#### Models and implementation details.

We use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib26)) as task
models. We evaluate two variants of SPLICE: SPLICE (Know. Evo), which
evolves knowledge with the task model fixed, and SPLICE (Co-Evo), which
co-evolves knowledge and the model with the asynchronous procedure in
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Asynchronous Co-Evolution ‣ Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
The knowledge optimizer is an external LLM, and each knowledge evolution
round uses three evolution views. Further implementation details and
hyperparameters are provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

### 4.2 Main Results

#### Knowledge evolution.

With the task model fixed, SPLICE (Know. Evo) matches or outperforms all
knowledge evolution baselines on every benchmark. It improves Avg. over
the strongest baseline, SkillOpt, by 6.6 and 7.1 points with Qwen3.5-4B
and Qwen3.5-9B, with the largest gains on WebShop (13.9 and 11.1
points), where tasks require long-horizon interaction with the
environment.

#### Knowledge-model co-evolution.

SPLICE (Co-Evo) achieves the highest Avg. among methods that update
model parameters, surpassing the strongest baseline, ReSkill, by 3.0 and
4.6 points with Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Notably, skill-augmented
baselines do not always improve over GRPO, suggesting that evolved
skills with inconsistent utility can interfere with policy learning on
complex tasks. SPLICE mitigates this issue by internalizing only
knowledge selected by utility consistency across evolution views.
Together, SPLICE couples consistency-regularized knowledge evolution
with model evolution, allowing the agent to benefit from useful external
guidance while continually improving its own policy.

### 4.3 Analysis

#### Effect of consistency regularization.

The central claim of SPLICE is that utility gains consistent across
evolution views provide stronger evidence for updating knowledge than
gains observed under a single view. We examine this claim by tracking
the proposed updates over 50 evolution rounds on WebShop, comparing
SPLICE (Know. Evo) with the knowledge evolution baselines.

| Model      | Metric            | Mean gain | Common gain |
|------------|-------------------|-----------|-------------|
| Qwen3.5-4B | Test Acc. (%)     | 44.40     | 58.20       |
|            | Gain$`\geq`$0 (%) | 28.57     | 67.86       |
| Qwen3.5-9B | Test Acc. (%)     | 53.60     | 59.67       |
|            | Gain$`\geq`$0 (%) | 28.57     | 69.05       |

Table 2: Common gain versus mean gain on WebShop. Mean gain scores task
evidence by the average utility gain across evolution views.
Gain$`\geq`$0 is the percentage of rounds in which validation Acc. is
not degraded.

As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Effect of consistency regularization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
(left), SPLICE reaches 53% and 49% validation Acc. by round 10 with
Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B and remains stable afterwards, whereas the
baselines fluctuate at lower levels.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Effect of consistency regularization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
(right) reports the fraction of rounds in which the proposed update
lowers validation Acc. by more than a given margin. Only 6% and 2% of
the updates proposed by SPLICE cause drops larger than 5 points with
Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, compared with up to 46% and 56% for the
baselines. Consistency across evolution views thus makes updates less
likely to degrade the current knowledge, in line with
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Improvement under a new evolution view). ‣ Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

Figure 3: Validation performance and degradation risk on WebShop. Left:
validation Acc. of the proposed update across evolution rounds, before
acceptance. Right: percentage of rounds in which the proposed update
causes an absolute validation Acc. drop larger than a given threshold
(in points).

tasks, i.e., total output tokens divided by the number of correct

Figure 4: Different strategies of using multiple evolution views on
SpreadSheet and WebShop. Best branch adopts the candidate with the
highest mean replay reward, and Merge-all updates knowledge with the
evidence from all tasks. SPLICE (Know. Evo) achieves the best
performance in all settings.

As an ablation,
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Effect of consistency regularization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
replaces common gain with mean gain when selecting task evidence. With
mean gain, Test Acc. drops by 13.8 and 6.1 points with Qwen3.5-4B and
Qwen3.5-9B, and validation Acc. is maintained or improved in only 29% of
rounds. The consistency term is thus essential to the effectiveness of
SPLICE.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Results ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
further analyzes how consistency affects the stability of individual
updates and their effects at the task level.

#### Beyond scaling computation.

SPLICE spends additional computation on generating multiple evolution
views and replaying their candidates. To examine whether its gains come
merely from this additional computation, we compare it with two variants
that also generate multiple evolution views but use them differently:
Best branch adopts the candidate with the highest mean replay reward,
and Merge-all updates knowledge with the evidence from all tasks without
selection by common gain. As shown in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Effect of consistency regularization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
SPLICE achieves the highest Test Acc. for both model sizes on
SpreadSheet and WebShop. Best branch performs worst, suggesting that
relying on a single view discards useful evidence, while the evidence
merged by Merge-all can be redundant or distracting. The gains of SPLICE
thus stem from how common gain uses the evolution views, not from the
additional computation alone.

#### Efficiency.

Although SPLICE draws on multiple knowledge candidates in each round, we
expect its knowledge to be compact but effective, because it retains
only updates supported by consistent utility gains across evolution
views. To examine whether this holds, we measure the final knowledge
length of SPLICE (Know. Evo) and the knowledge evolution baselines,
together with the average output tokens and interaction steps over all
WebShop test attempts, including failures. As shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Efficiency. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
SPLICE produces knowledge of 4.98k and 6.07k tokens for Qwen3.5-4B and
Qwen3.5-9B, respectively, compared with ACE’s 41.51k and 64.99k. Its
knowledge is also shorter than EvoSkill’s but longer than SkillOpt’s.
SPLICE requires the fewest interaction steps (8.33 and 8.64), suggesting
that task-solving efficiency depends on the retained guidance as well as
knowledge length. ACE produces shorter outputs with Qwen3.5-4B, but with
much longer knowledge and more interaction steps.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Figure 4 ‣ Effect of consistency regularization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
further reports the output tokens per correct attempt, which measures
the cost of obtaining a correct solution. SPLICE has the lowest value on
both WebShop and LiveCode for both model sizes, reducing it by up to 44%
relative to the strongest baseline, indicating that it improves accuracy
while reducing the cost of obtaining correct solutions.

Figure 5: Knowledge length, output tokens, and interaction steps on
WebShop. Results of SPLICE (Know. Evo) and knowledge evolution baselines
with Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. ReasoningBank uses a dynamic knowledge
bank, so its knowledge length is omitted.

#### Knowledge generalization.

Just as consistency regularization improves model generalization, we
expect utility consistency to yield knowledge that generalizes across
task models. To examine whether this holds, we take the final knowledge
evolved with Qwen3.5-9B by SPLICE (Know. Evo) and the knowledge
evolution baselines, and apply it without further evolution to task
models of other sizes (Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-27B) and other families
(Gemma-4-12B-IT ([Gemma Team, 2026](#bib.bib45)) and
Muse-Glimmer-30B ([Meta Superintelligence Lab, 2026](#bib.bib46))). We
measure absolute Test Acc. gains (in points) over each target model
without knowledge on LiveMath and SpreadSheet. As shown in
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Knowledge generalization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
SPLICE yields the largest mean gain in all settings. On LiveMath, its
advantage over the baselines is particularly large for Qwen3.5-4B and
Gemma-4-12B-IT: the gains are 31.13 and 33.86 points, respectively,
compared with at most 17.38 and 12.42 points for the baselines. Notably,
the gains of SPLICE on LiveMath remain at a similar level across all
four target models, whereas those of the baselines drop substantially on
Qwen3.5-4B and Gemma-4-12B-IT, indicating that the knowledge evolved by
SPLICE is less sensitive to which model uses it.

Figure 6: Generalization across model sizes and families. Knowledge
evolved with Qwen3.5-9B is applied to other task models without further
evolution. Bars show absolute gains in avg@8 Test Acc. (in points) over
the same model without knowledge; error bars show paired 95% confidence
intervals.

Figure 7: Model and knowledge contributions on LiveMath. Test Acc. of
base and trained models evaluated without knowledge, with the knowledge
at the start of training (Early $`K`$), and with the final knowledge
(Final $`K`$).

#### Co-evolution dynamics.

Co-evolution trains the model with the evolved knowledge, which raises
two questions: whether the model internalizes the knowledge, and how the
utility of knowledge changes as the model evolves.
Figure [7](#S4.F7.fig1 "Figure 7 ‣ Knowledge generalization. ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
evaluates base and trained models on LiveMath with knowledge from
different stages. For the first question, the trained models without
knowledge already outperform the base models equipped with the final
knowledge for both model sizes, reaching 67.88% versus 52.32% with
Qwen3.5-9B, indicating that model evolution internalizes and extends the
evolved knowledge. For the second question, knowledge brings much
smaller gains to the trained models than to the base models, and the
early knowledge no longer improves the trained 4B model. The training
dynamics in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Results ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
show the same trend during training: the benefit of the current
knowledge shrinks as the model improves without it. Validating knowledge
with the current model before using it for training therefore keeps
model evolution from internalizing knowledge that no longer helps.

## 5 Related Work

#### Knowledge evolution for LLM agents.

LLM agents improve without parameter updates by turning experience into
external knowledge, from textual reflections ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) to structured
memories, playbooks, and skills that are continually updated ([Ouyang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8); [Alzubi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6); [Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib40)). As such knowledge accumulates, recent studies find
that it does not reliably improve task performance ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib14); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Dong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)) and that seemingly correct experience can mislead
future tasks ([Xiong et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). Some methods therefore
retain only updates with positive estimated gain ([Tang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib49)), evaluating each candidate on its own. Rather than
relying on any single analysis, SPLICE uses utility consistency across
evolution views to guide knowledge evolution.

#### Knowledge internalization and co-evolution.

Knowledge can also be internalized into model parameters through
reinforcement learning and self-distillation ([Lu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9); [Lu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10); [He et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib13); [Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)), or evolved together
with the policy ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [He et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib12); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Shi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)). Meanwhile, on-policy self-distillation, in which the
model conditioned on privileged context serves as its own teacher ([Zhao
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)), has been refined with token-level
modulation ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib48)) and contrastive references
([Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). SPLICE constructs its contrastive
reference from knowledge that consistently degrades utility during
knowledge evolution, and gates it at the token level to retain guidance
shared with the evolved knowledge.

#### Consistency regularization.

Consistency regularization improves generalization by encouraging
consistent predictions for the same input under perturbations. It was
first widely adopted in semi-supervised learning ([Bachman et al.,
2014](#bib.bib33); [Sajjadi et al., 2016](#bib.bib34); [Tarvainen and
Valpola, 2017](#bib.bib37); [Xie et al., 2020](#bib.bib36)) and has
since been extended to supervised training and fine-tuning of large
models ([Wu et al., 2021](#bib.bib17); [Ni et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)).
Inspired by this idea, SPLICE applies consistency to the utility of
evolved knowledge. Additional related work is discussed in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C More Related Work ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

## 6 Conclusion

We introduce SPLICE, a framework for consistency-regularized
knowledge-model co-evolution. SPLICE updates knowledge based on utility
gains that are consistent across evolution views and internalizes the
evolved knowledge through reinforcement learning and gated contrastive
self-distillation. Across four benchmarks and two model scales, SPLICE
outperforms knowledge evolution and model training baselines, while its
evolved knowledge enables more efficient task solving and transfers
across model sizes and families. Overall, our results suggest that
utility gains consistent across different ways of analyzing experience,
rather than those observed under any single analysis, provide an
effective signal for turning experience into generalizable knowledge
that, when internalized through model evolution, supports long-term
agentic evolution.

## Appendix

## Appendix A Implementation Details

### A.1 Benchmarks

Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Benchmarks ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
summarizes the data splits. Training tasks provide experience for
knowledge evolution and model training, validation tasks are used to
evaluate proposed knowledge updates, and test tasks are used only for
evaluation.

| Benchmark   | Train | Val. | Test | Output tokens | Epochs |
|-------------|-------|------|------|---------------|--------|
| LiveMath    | 86    | 43   | 302  | 16,384        | 3      |
| LiveCode    | 68    | 34   | 240  | 32,768        | 3      |
| SpreadSheet | 80    | 40   | 280  | 4,096         | 3      |
| WebShop     | 1,000 | 100  | 500  | 512           | 1      |

Table 4: Data splits and training settings. Counts refer to tasks, or
shopping sessions for WebShop. Output tokens are the maximum number of
tokens per model response.

#### LiveMath.

We use LiveMathematicianBench ([He et al., 2026a](#bib.bib22)) in its
multiple-choice setting without proof sketches, with problems from the
March–June 2026 subsets. The agent answers each problem by selecting one
of five options.

#### LiveCode.

We use the code-generation subset of LiveCodeBench ([Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23)), combining the v5 and v6 releases and splitting
problems by contest so that no contest is shared across splits. The
agent writes a Python solution, which is evaluated by the
execution-based test runner of LiveCodeBench.

#### SpreadSheet.

We use the Verified-400 subset of SpreadsheetBench ([Ma et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24)). Given an instruction and an input workbook, the
agent writes Python code to produce an output workbook and can revise
the code using execution feedback.

#### WebShop.

We use the official 1K-product environment with synthetic shopping
goals ([Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib25)). The agent navigates textual
product pages through search and click actions, including product-option
selection and purchase.

### A.2 Models and Baselines

#### Models.

The task models are Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team,
2026](#bib.bib26)) with thinking mode disabled, decoded with temperature
1.0, top-$`p`$ 0.95, and top-$`k`$ 20. The knowledge optimizer is an
external LLM.
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Models. ‣ A.2 Models and Baselines ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
lists the hyperparameters of SPLICE.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Component | Hyperparameter | Value |
| Knowledge evolution | Evolution views $`N`$ | 3 |
|  | Replay runs per candidate | 1 |
|  | Selected tasks $`n`$ | $`\{1,2,3\}`$ |
| Model evolution | Self-distillation weight $`\lambda`$ | $`\{0.1,0.3,0.5,1\}`$ |
|  | Learning rate | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ |
|  | Training batch size | 8 |
|  | Group size | 16 (LiveMath), 8 (others) |
| Co-evolution | Reward-gap thresholds $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{sd}}=\epsilon_{\mathrm{end}}`$ | 0.03 |
|  | Stage budgets $`T_{\min}`$, $`T_{\max}`$ | 3, 5 (WebShop: 10, 20) |
|  | Restart patience $`L`$ | 2 |
|  | Warmup rounds | 4 (WebShop, LiveMath), 8 (others) |

Table 5: Hyperparameters of SPLICE.

#### Baselines.

Base uses the task model without knowledge. ReasoningBank ([Ouyang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib4)) stores reasoning memories distilled from
experience and retrieves task-relevant entries. ACE ([Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib8)) maintains an evolving playbook through reflection and
curation. EvoSkill ([Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)) builds skills from
task experience, and SkillOpt ([Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7))
iteratively optimizes external skills. GRPO ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)) trains the task model with group-relative policy
optimization, and SkillRL ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)) and
ReSkill ([He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib12)) combine skill evolution with
policy optimization. All training-based methods are trained for the
number of epochs listed in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Benchmarks ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

### A.3 Evaluation Protocol

We report accuracy (Acc.), the percentage of test tasks that are solved.
A task is solved if the selected option is correct on LiveMath, all test
cases pass on LiveCode, the output workbook matches the reference in all
cases on SpreadSheet, or the purchase receives the full reward on
WebShop. Results of training-free methods are averaged over three seeds.
SPLICE (Co-Evo) evaluates the final model with the latest knowledge that
passes held-out validation with this model, and without knowledge if no
knowledge passes.

## Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution

### B.1 Design Considerations

Knowledge evolution and model evolution depend on each other. The
utility of knowledge depends on the model that uses it: guidance that
helps the current model can become redundant or even harmful after the
model is trained. Model evolution, in turn, internalizes knowledge
through self-distillation from the model conditioned on it, which
requires the knowledge to remain fixed. Co-evolution therefore has two
requirements:

- •
  (R1) knowledge is evaluated with the model that uses it;
- •
  (R2) $`K`$ and $`K^{-}`$ remain fixed while the model internalizes
  them.

A further consideration is efficiency. Knowledge evolution typically
requires multiple rounds before it produces stable knowledge with clear
utility gains. If model evolution waits for these rounds, training
stalls; if it uses knowledge too early, it internalizes weak guidance.
The two procedures below handle this trade-off differently. The
sequential procedure waits and satisfies both requirements exactly,
whereas the asynchronous procedure relaxes R1 during knowledge evolution
so that training uses knowledge as soon as it proves useful.

### B.2 Sequential Co-Evolution

The sequential procedure
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ B.2 Sequential Co-Evolution ‣ Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"))
alternates the two processes. Knowledge evolution runs with the model
fixed, so every candidate is replayed and validated with the model that
will use it. It continues until $`M`$ consecutive updates are rejected,
indicating that knowledge evolution no longer improves the knowledge
under the current model. Model evolution then performs $`T`$ updates
with $`K`$ and $`K^{-}`$ fixed. The rejected rounds share the same model
and knowledge, and thus provide a common baseline for constructing
$`K^{-}`$ from consistent utility degradation
(§ [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")).
Afterwards, knowledge evolution continues from the current $`K`$ with
experience collected by the updated model.

This procedure satisfies R1 and R2 exactly, but each process waits for
the other: training is idle during the multiple rounds of knowledge
evolution, and knowledge evolution is idle during training.

1: Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, rejection threshold $`M`$, model-update
budget $`T`$, total budget.

2: Initialize $`K\leftarrow\varnothing`$.

3: while total budget remains do

4:   \[Knowledge Evolution\]

5:   repeat

6:    Collect experience $`\mathcal{E}`$ using $`\pi_{\theta}`$
conditioned on $`K`$.

7:    Generate knowledge candidates $`\{K^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{N}`$.
$`\triangleright`$
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")

8:    Replay tasks and compute common gains. $`\triangleright`$
Eq. [3](#S3.E3 "In Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")

9:    Construct $`\widetilde{K}`$ from the selected tasks.
$`\triangleright`$
Eq. [5](#S3.E5 "In Knowledge evolution from common gain. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")

10:    Accept $`K\leftarrow\widetilde{K}`$ if held-out validation
performance improves.

11:   until $`M`$ consecutive updates are rejected or the total budget
is exhausted

12:   \[Model Evolution\]

13:   Construct $`K^{-}`$ from consistent utility degradation in the
last $`M`$ rejected rounds.

14:   for up to $`T`$ updates within the remaining budget do

15:    Collect trajectories with and without $`K`$.

16:    Update $`\theta`$ with $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPLICE}}`$.
$`\triangleright`$
Eq. [7](#S3.E7 "In Gated knowledge internalization. ‣ 3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")

17:   end for

18: end while

19: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and $`K`$.

### B.3 Asynchronous Co-Evolution

The asynchronous procedure
(Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ Restarting knowledge evolution. ‣ B.3 Asynchronous Co-Evolution ‣ Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"))
runs knowledge evolution and model evolution at the same time. Knowledge
evolution keeps improving its own copy of knowledge,
$`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$, using experience generated during training, while
model evolution trains with $`K`$, the most recent $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$
that improves held-out validation performance with the current model.
Useful knowledge thus enters training without waiting for knowledge
evolution to stop, and training does not stall. Before training starts,
knowledge evolution runs several rounds with the initial model to obtain
initial knowledge.

#### Consistent references for comparison.

Training experience is generated under whichever knowledge the current
stage uses. Knowledge evolution therefore takes trajectories generated
under the same knowledge $`K^{\prime}`$ and measures replay gains
relative to $`K^{\prime}`$. Updates supported by common gain are merged
into the latest $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$, which can differ from
$`K^{\prime}`$; knowledge evolution therefore accumulates improvements
instead of restarting with each batch.

#### Adopting knowledge for training.

Model evolution proceeds in training stages. At the start of each stage,
the latest $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$ is compared with no knowledge on the
held-out validation set using the current model. It is adopted as $`K`$
only if it improves validation performance; otherwise, the stage trains
with GRPO alone. Each stage that trains with $`K`$ first constructs
$`K^{-}`$ from the replay results of recent knowledge evolution rounds
by selecting tasks with consistent utility degradation using
$`-\Delta_{ij}`$
(§ [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Knowledge-Guided Model Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")).
Because knowledge evolution evaluates candidates with earlier models,
validating with the current model restores R1 at the time of adoption.
Within a stage, $`K`$ and $`K^{-}`$ remain fixed, which satisfies R2.

#### When to replace the training knowledge.

The batch reward gap, i.e., the mean of
$`\overline{R}_{i}^{K}-\overline{R}_{i}^{\varnothing}`$ over a batch,
measures how much of the benefit of $`K`$ the model has not yet
internalized. Self-distillation is applied only when this gap exceeds
$`\epsilon_{\mathrm{sd}}`$, which extends the task-level weight
$`w_{i}`$ to the batch level; other batches use GRPO alone. A stage ends
once the gap falls to $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{end}}`$ or below after at
least $`T_{\min}`$ updates, indicating that $`K`$ has been largely
internalized, or after $`T_{\max}`$ updates, so that newer knowledge can
be adopted. A stage without knowledge ends after $`T_{\min}`$ updates.
$`T_{\min}`$ keeps each stage long enough for stable training, while
$`T_{\max}`$ limits how long training relies on outdated knowledge.

#### Restarting knowledge evolution.

If no knowledge is adopted for $`L`$ consecutive stages, which indicates
that the knowledge accumulated in $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$ no longer helps
the current model, knowledge evolution restarts from empty knowledge
while keeping the current model and the collected experience. At the end
of training, the latest $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$ is validated with the final
model in the same way to determine the returned knowledge.

1: Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$; reward-gap thresholds
$`\epsilon_{\mathrm{sd}}`$ and $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{end}}`$; stage
budgets $`T_{\min}\leq T_{\max}`$; restart patience $`L`$; total budget.

2: Run knowledge evolution with the initial model to obtain
$`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$.

3: Run the two processes below at the same time.

4: \[Knowledge Evolution\]

5: while training continues do

6:   Take training experience generated under the same knowledge.

7:   Run knowledge evolution on it
(§ [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"))
and update $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$.

8:   Restart from $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}\leftarrow\varnothing`$ if
requested.

9: end while

10: \[Model Evolution\]

11: while total budget remains do

12:   Adopt $`K\leftarrow K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$ if it improves validation
performance with the current model; otherwise
$`K\leftarrow\varnothing`$.

13:   If $`K\neq\varnothing`$, construct $`K^{-}`$ from consistent
utility degradation in recent rounds before training.

14:   Request a restart after $`L`$ consecutive stages without adopted
knowledge.

15:   repeat

16:    Collect trajectories with and without $`K`$; pass them to
knowledge evolution.

17:    Update $`\theta`$ with $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPLICE}}`$ if the
reward gap exceeds $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{sd}}`$; otherwise with
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}`$.

18:   until the gap is at most $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{end}}`$ after
$`T_{\min}`$ updates, or $`T_{\max}`$ updates are reached

19: end while

20: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$, and $`K_{\mathrm{evo}}`$ if it improves
validation performance with the final model.

Algorithm 2 SPLICE: Asynchronous Co-Evolution

### B.4 Discussion: Relaxing R1

In the asynchronous procedure, the model is updated while knowledge
evolution runs, so replay can use a newer model than the one that
generated the experience. For task $`x_{i}`$, the replay gain then
decomposes as $`\Delta_{ij}=\Delta^{*}_{ij}+b_{i}`$, where
$`\Delta^{*}_{ij}`$ is the gain of $`K^{(j)}`$ measured with the replay
model alone, and $`b_{i}`$ is the reward change caused by the model
update under the knowledge that generated the experience. Since all
candidates for $`x_{i}`$ are replayed with the same model, $`b_{i}`$ is
shared across views, and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{C}_{i}=\frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{j<\ell}\min(\Delta^{*}_{ij},\Delta^{*}_{i\ell})+b_{i}.
``` |  | (8) |

The inconsistency penalty is unchanged, so the comparison among
evolution views remains valid. The shift instead changes which tasks
pass the threshold $`\widehat{C}_{i}>0`$: model improvement
($`b_{i}>0`$) admits tasks whose gains come from training rather than
from knowledge, and model degradation ($`b_{i}<0`$) excludes useful
evidence.
Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Improvement under a new evolution view). ‣ Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
likewise assumes a fixed model.

Two design choices limit this effect. Knowledge evolution uses recent
experience, which keeps the model change between experience collection
and replay small. More importantly, knowledge enters training only after
it improves validation performance over no knowledge with the current
model, so an update whose apparent gain comes from the model update is
not adopted unless it also helps the current model. The remaining cost
is efficiency: a shifted threshold can select less informative tasks and
produce updates that are later rejected. Compared with the sequential
procedure, the asynchronous procedure accepts this cost in exchange for
using knowledge without waiting for knowledge evolution to finish.

## Appendix C More Related Work

#### Knowledge evolution for LLM agents.

LLM agents can improve without parameter updates by turning experience
into external knowledge. Early methods reflect on failures and store
textual lessons: Reflexion keeps verbal self-reflections for subsequent
attempts ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib1)), ExpeL extracts insights from
successful and failed trajectories across tasks ([Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)), CLIN maintains a textual memory updated across trials
([Majumder et al., 2023](#bib.bib3)), and Agent-Pro reflects at the
level of the agent’s policy ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)). Another
line accumulates procedural knowledge, such as executable skill
libraries ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib27)), workflows induced from past
trajectories ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)), and skills that are
automatically discovered and refined ([Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib6);
[Yang et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)),
including learnable memory operations ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib40)). Other methods maintain structured memories or
contexts that evolve during task solving, including agentic memory
organization ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)), adaptive test-time memory
([Suzgun et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)), reasoning strategies distilled from
successes and failures ([Ouyang et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), and evolving
playbooks ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)). Training-Free GRPO further
distills experiential knowledge from group-relative comparisons of
rollouts ([Cai et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)). Related studies examine the
reliability of skills and agentic reasoning: model-generated skills do
not reliably improve performance ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib14); [Huang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib50)), unchecked
accumulation degrades skill retrieval ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib44)), and agents can fail to use experience and external
evidence reliably ([Xiong et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Zhao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib51)). Some methods therefore retain only updates with
positive estimated gain ([Tang et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)). SPLICE
focuses on which evidence should drive a knowledge update, using utility
consistency across multiple evolution views of the same experience.

#### Knowledge internalization and co-evolution.

Internalizing knowledge into model parameters is closely related to
context distillation, which trains a model without a context to match
its predictions with the context ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib31)), and
to on-policy distillation, which supervises a student on its own
generated trajectories ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib32)). For LLM
agents, recent work internalizes skills into the policy through
reinforcement learning and self-distillation ([Lu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9); [He et al., 2026c](#bib.bib13)), progressively
reduces reliance on skills provided in context ([Lu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib10)), or attributes success to skills by contrasting
rollouts with and without them ([Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). Other
work evolves knowledge together with the policy: skill banks are updated
during online reinforcement learning ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)),
skill creation is coupled with policy optimization ([He et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib12)), experience is distilled into principles that guide
further policy learning ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)), and a single
policy learns to select, use, and distill skills ([Shi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib41)). On-policy self-distillation, in which the model
conditioned on privileged context serves as its own teacher, has become
a dense training signal for LLMs ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib20)).
Since privileged context can distort the teacher’s token distribution,
recent variants modulate token-level guidance by teacher–student
disagreement ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib48)), reverse the distillation
direction ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)), or contrast signals under
correct and wrong hints ([Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). Negative
signals have likewise been shown to provide useful supervision in
reinforcement learning for LLMs ([Zhu et al., 2026](#bib.bib21)). SPLICE
derives its negative reference from knowledge evolution itself, using
knowledge associated with consistent utility degradation, and combines
it with task-level weighting and a token-level gate during
internalization.

#### Consistency regularization.

Consistency regularization encourages a model to make consistent
predictions for the same input under perturbations. In semi-supervised
learning, early methods enforce agreement under stochastic
transformations, dropout, and ensembling ([Bachman et al.,
2014](#bib.bib33); [Sajjadi et al., 2016](#bib.bib34); [Laine and Aila,
2016](#bib.bib35)), and later methods improve the targets with
weight-averaged teachers ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#bib.bib37)) or
strong data augmentation ([Xie et al., 2020](#bib.bib36)). The idea has
been extended to supervised training and fine-tuning through consistency
between dropout sub-models ([Wu et al., 2021](#bib.bib17)) or under
parameter perturbations ([Ni et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)). These methods
assume that the correct output is invariant to the perturbation and
enforce consistency through a training loss. In knowledge evolution,
this assumption does not hold at the level of content, since different
evolution views are expected to produce different knowledge. SPLICE
therefore requires consistency only in the utility gains of the
resulting knowledge and uses it as a criterion for selecting evidence.

This section provides additional analyses of consistency regularization
and knowledge-model co-evolution, complementing

Figure 8: Validation gains of proposed updates on WebShop. Validation
Acc. of the proposed update minus that of the current knowledge (in
points) at each evolution round, including rejected updates. Insets show
the mean absolute change.

#### Stability of proposed updates.

Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix D Additional Results ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
reports the change in validation Acc. caused by the proposed update at
each of the first 50 evolution rounds on WebShop, including updates that
are later rejected. The baselines frequently propose updates that lower
validation Acc. by 10 points or more, especially SkillOpt and EvoSkill.
In contrast, the updates proposed by SPLICE mostly stay close to zero or
positive and have the smallest mean absolute change for both model
sizes. This is consistent with the design of common gain, which
discounts evidence whose gains appear under only some evolution views
and thus avoids updates that change the knowledge in unstable ways.

Figure 9: Error correction and success preservation on WebShop.
Percentages of tasks failed under the current knowledge that a proposed
update solves, and of solved tasks that remain solved. Small points
denote proposed updates in the first 30 rounds; large markers show
pooled rates.

#### Error correction and success preservation.

To examine how proposed updates affect individual tasks, we compare each
proposed update with the current knowledge on the validation tasks.
Error correction is the percentage of tasks failed under the current
knowledge that the proposed update solves, and success preservation is
the percentage of tasks solved under the current knowledge that remain
solved.
Figure [9](#A4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Stability of proposed updates. ‣ Appendix D Additional Results ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
reports both metrics for the proposed updates in the first 30 evolution
rounds on WebShop, excluding rounds without an update. SPLICE attains
the highest pooled rates for both metrics: 23.60% error correction and
75.94% success preservation with Qwen3.5-4B, and 17.75% and 77.47% with
Qwen3.5-9B, whereas the best baseline preservation rates are 68.40% and
64.79%. Updates selected by common gain thus correct more errors while
breaking fewer existing successes.

#### Training dynamics of co-evolution.

Figure [10](#A4.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Error correction and success preservation. ‣ Appendix D Additional Results ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
(left) tracks validation Acc. on LiveMath during co-evolution,
evaluating the model without knowledge and with the latest knowledge at
each optimizer update step. Early in training, the knowledge improves
the model substantially. As the model improves without knowledge, this
benefit shrinks, and some knowledge updates no longer improve the
current model and are rejected. The examples on the right illustrate
both directions of this interplay. For the 4B model, the same knowledge
helps the model answer correctly at update step 44, but by update step
56 the model answers correctly without it, whereas adding the knowledge
leads to an error. For the 9B model, a check learned from execution
feedback corrects an unsupported convergence claim on another task: at
update step 32, the model answers incorrectly without knowledge and
correctly with it, and the knowledge is accepted for subsequent
training. These dynamics motivate validating knowledge with the current
model before using it for training
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")).

## Appendix E Proof of Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Improvement under a new evolution view). ‣ Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

All expectations and probabilities below are over evolution views, with
the task, experience, model, and current knowledge fixed. Recall that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu=\mathbb{E}[\Delta],\qquad C=\mathbb{E}[\min(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime})].
``` |  |

The assumption $`\mathbb{E}|\Delta|<\infty`$ and identical distributions
ensure that $`C`$ is finite, since
$`|\min(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime})|\leq|\Delta|+|\Delta^{\prime}|`$.
Furthermore, $`\min(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime})\leq\Delta`$ implies
$`C\leq\mu`$. Thus, $`C>0`$ ensures $`\mu>0`$.

We establish a more general bound for any threshold $`0\leq a<C`$. The
following pointwise inequality holds:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\min(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime})-a\leq(\Delta-a)\mathbf{1}\{\Delta^{\prime}>a\}.
``` |  | (9) |

If $`\Delta^{\prime}\leq a`$, the left-hand side is at most
$`\Delta^{\prime}-a\leq 0`$, while the right-hand side is zero. If
$`\Delta^{\prime}>a`$, the right-hand side equals $`\Delta-a`$, which is
at least $`\min(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime})-a`$.

Taking expectations and using independence gives

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle C-a`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\Delta-a)\mathbf{1}\{\Delta^{\prime}>a\}\right]`$ |  | (10) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Delta-a]\Pr(\Delta^{\prime}>a)`$ |  | (11) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=(\mu-a)\Pr(\Delta>a),`$ |  | (12) |

where the last equality follows from the identical distributions of
$`\Delta`$ and $`\Delta^{\prime}`$. Since $`\mu\geq C>a`$, we obtain

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr(\Delta>a)\geq\frac{C-a}{\mu-a},\qquad\Pr(\Delta\leq a)\leq\frac{\mu-C}{\mu-a}.
``` |  | (13) |

Setting $`a=0`$ yields

|     |                                 |     |
|-----|---------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Pr(\Delta>0)\geq\frac{C}{\mu}.
       ```                              |     |

Finally, using $`\min(u,v)=(u+v-|u-v|)/2`$, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\Delta]+\mathbb{E}[\Delta^{\prime}]-\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|}{2}=\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|.
``` |  |

Therefore,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Pr(\Delta>0)\geq\frac{C}{\mu}=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|}{2\mu},
``` |  |

which completes the proof. ∎

## Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection

### F.1 Illustrative Comparison of Selection Strategies

We use a simplified model to examine how different selection strategies
respond to utility gains that are specific to particular evolution
views. All strategies use the same knowledge optimizer and the same
budget: each selects the evidence of one task and constructs one
knowledge update from it. This comparison isolates the selection of task
evidence from how the knowledge optimizer consolidates updates.

Consider two replayed tasks, $`R`$ and $`S`$. The knowledge updates
constructed from their evidence have expected utility gains
$`g_{R}>g_{S}>0`$ on held-out tasks, relative to the current knowledge
$`K`$. Across $`N\geq 2`$ independently sampled evolution views, their
replay gains satisfy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{Rj}=g_{R},\qquad\Delta_{Sj}=g_{S}+aZ_{j},\qquad Z_{j}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q),\quad j=1,\ldots,N,
``` |  | (14) |

where $`0<q<1`$. The term $`aZ_{j}`$ represents a view-specific gain
that appears on the replayed task under only some evolution views. We
assume that this gain does not transfer to held-out tasks. Let
$`d=g_{R}-g_{S}`$ and assume $`a>d>0`$, so that an individual view can
rank $`S`$ above $`R`$ despite its lower held-out utility. To isolate
this effect, we treat the replay gains as exact expected reward
differences, without replay estimation noise.

Single-view selection ranks the tasks by $`\Delta_{i1}`$. Mean-gain
selection ranks them by $`\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Delta_{ij}`$.
Common-gain selection uses
Eq. [3](#S3.E3 "In Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
After selection, the same knowledge optimizer constructs the update from
the evidence of the selected task. For definiteness, ties are resolved
in favor of $`R`$.

Let $`H=\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j}`$ denote the number of views under which
$`S`$ receives the additional gain. Then
$`H\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,q)`$, and the mean-gain and common-gain
scores of $`S`$ are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle s_{S}^{\mathrm{mean}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=g_{S}+a\frac{H}{N},`$ |  | (15) |
|  | $`\displaystyle s_{S}^{\mathrm{common}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=g_{S}+a\frac{H(H-1)}{N(N-1)}.`$ |  |  |

The second expression follows because only pairs in which both views
receive the additional gain contribute $`a`$ to the pairwise minimum.
Task $`R`$ has score $`g_{R}`$ under all selection strategies.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

Since $`a>d`$, single-view selection chooses $`S`$ exactly when
$`Z_{1}=1`$, with probability $`q`$. For the other two strategies,
Eq. [15](#A6.E15 "In F.1 Illustrative Comparison of Selection Strategies ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
gives

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Pr(\text{mean selects }S)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\frac{H}{N}>\frac{d}{a}\right),`$ |  | (19) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Pr(\text{common selects }S)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\frac{H(H-1)}{N(N-1)}>\frac{d}{a}\right).`$ |  |  |

For every $`H\in\{0,\ldots,N\}`$,

|     |                                       |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \frac{H(H-1)}{N(N-1)}\leq\frac{H}{N}.
       ```                                    |     |

Therefore, whenever common-gain selection chooses $`S`$, mean-gain
selection also chooses $`S`$. Selecting $`S`$ instead of $`R`$ reduces
held-out utility by $`d>0`$, proving
Eq. [16](#A6.E16 "In Proposition 2 (Selection under view-specific gains). ‣ F.1 Illustrative Comparison of Selection Strategies ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").

By the law of large numbers,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{H}{N}\longrightarrow q,\qquad\frac{H(H-1)}{N(N-1)}\longrightarrow q^{2}
``` |  |

almost surely. Under
Eq. [17](#A6.E17 "In Proposition 2 (Selection under view-specific gains). ‣ F.1 Illustrative Comparison of Selection Strategies ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization"),
the probability that mean-gain selection chooses $`S`$ converges to one,
while the corresponding probability for common-gain selection converges
to zero. The expected held-out utility of any selection rule is
$`g_{R}-d\Pr(\text{select }S)`$. Substitution yields
Eq. [18](#A6.E18 "In Proposition 2 (Selection under view-specific gains). ‣ F.1 Illustrative Comparison of Selection Strategies ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
Because $`0<q<1`$ and $`d>0`$, $`g_{R}>g_{R}-dq>g_{S}`$, establishing
the strict comparison for sufficiently large $`N`$. ∎

This example distinguishes collecting more views from requiring utility
consistency across them. As $`N`$ increases, mean-gain selection more
accurately estimates $`g_{S}+aq`$, which still includes the
view-specific gain. Common gain instead approaches $`g_{S}+aq^{2}`$,
reducing the contribution of gains supported by only a fraction of the
views. When $`aq^{2}<d<aq`$, this difference changes which task evidence
is selected for the knowledge update.

The advantage depends on both the transfer assumption and the relative
size of the view-specific gain. If $`d>aq`$, both multi-view strategies
select $`R`$ with probability approaching one. If $`d<aq^{2}`$, both
select $`S`$ with probability approaching one. The analysis therefore
illustrates a regime in which consistency helps identify more
transferable updates; it does not establish universal superiority over
mean-gain selection or merging all evidence.

### F.2 Robustness to Shifts in Evolution Views

Proposition [1](#Thmproposition1 "Proposition 1 (Improvement under a new evolution view). ‣ Knowledge consistency evaluation. ‣ 3.1 Consistency-Regularized Knowledge Evolution ‣ 3 SPLICE: Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
considers a new evolution view drawn from the same distribution. We now
allow the distribution of views to change, capturing shifts in how
experience is analyzed and transformed into knowledge.

Fix a task $`x_{i}`$, experience $`\mathcal{E}`$, model $`\theta`$, and
current knowledge $`K`$. Let $`P`$ denote the original distribution of
evolution views, and let $`\Delta(v)`$ be the expected reward gain of
the knowledge candidate produced under view $`v`$. Define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu=\mathbb{E}_{V\sim P}[\Delta(V)],\qquad C=\mathbb{E}_{V,V^{\prime}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}P}\left[\min(\Delta(V),\Delta(V^{\prime}))\right].
``` |  |

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

###### Proof.

Since $`w`$ is a density ratio, $`\mathbb{E}_{P}[w]=1`$.
Condition [20](#A6.E20 "In Proposition 3 (Utility under a shift in evolution views). ‣ F.2 Robustness to Shifts in Evolution Views ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
therefore implies $`0\leq w\leq 1+\rho`$ almost surely under $`P`$.
Consequently, $`\Delta`$ is integrable under $`Q`$, and

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\Delta]=\mathbb{E}_{P}[w\Delta]=\mu+\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(\Delta,w).
``` |  |

Let $`V,V^{\prime}`$ be independent draws from $`P`$, and write
$`\Delta=\Delta(V)`$, $`\Delta^{\prime}=\Delta(V^{\prime})`$,
$`w=w(V)`$, and $`w^{\prime}=w(V^{\prime})`$. The covariance identity
gives

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(\Delta,w)=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(\Delta-\Delta^{\prime})(w-w^{\prime})\right].
``` |  |

Because $`|w-w^{\prime}|\leq\rho`$ almost surely,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{Cov}_{P}(\Delta,w)\geq-\frac{\rho}{2}\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|.
``` |  |

Using $`C=\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}|\Delta-\Delta^{\prime}|`$, we obtain

|     |                                            |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathbb{E}_{Q}[\Delta]\geq\mu-\rho(\mu-C),
       ```                                         |     |

which proves
Eq. [21](#A6.E21 "In Proposition 3 (Utility under a shift in evolution views). ‣ F.2 Robustness to Shifts in Evolution Views ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization").
Finally, $`C\leq\mu`$, so for $`0\leq\rho\leq 1`$,

|     |                           |     |
|-----|---------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (1-\rho)\mu+\rho C\geq C.
       ```                        |     |

∎

The parameter $`\rho`$ controls how strongly the relative frequencies of
evolution views can change. For example, $`w(v)\in[1/2,3/2]`$ satisfies
Eq. [20](#A6.E20 "In Proposition 3 (Utility under a shift in evolution views). ‣ F.2 Robustness to Shifts in Evolution Views ‣ Appendix F Discussion of Common-Gain Selection ‣ Agentic Knowledge-Model Co-Evolution via Consistency Regularization")
with $`\rho=1`$. The bound shows that the possible reduction in expected
utility is controlled by $`\mu-C`$, the utility inconsistency. At a
fixed mean gain, lower inconsistency therefore provides a stronger
guarantee under a change in the view distribution.

This result concerns the utility of knowledge evolution on a fixed task.
It allows bounded reweighting of views supported by $`P`$; it does not
directly establish transfer to arbitrary new tasks or preservation of
utility after the knowledge optimizer consolidates updates.
````
